problem: Consider a spherical giant moon with radius $(5.9\times {10}^{11})\,\text{m}$ and surface gravitational acceleration $g=9.2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Which differential equation best models the velocity $v$ of an object projected radially outward from the  giant moon, where $r$ is the distance from the giant moon's center to the object? Assume the only force acting on the object is the force due to gravity.
worked_solution:
According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the magnitude of the inward gravitational force pulling the object toward the giant moon is

$$
{F}_{\text{in}}=G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}},
$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $m$ is the object's mass, and $M$ is the giant moon's mass.

Since this is the only force and it acts inward, the resultant force, taking *outward* as positive, is $F=-{F}_{\text{in}}.$
Applying Newton's second law, $F=ma,$ where $a$ is the acceleration of the object, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =-{F}_{\text{in}} \\ ma & =-G\,\frac{mM}{{r}^{2}} \\ a & =-\frac{GM}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the square of the distance,

$$
a=-\frac{k}{{r}^{2}},
$$

with constant of proportionality $k=GM>0.$

When at the surface, $r=(5.9\times {10}^{11})\,\text{m},$ the acceleration of the object due to gravity is $a=-9.2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ Substituting into our previous equation, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-9.2 & =-\frac{k}{(5.9\times {10}^{11})^{2}} \\ k & =9.2\cdot (5.9\times {10}^{11})^{2} \\  & =9.2\cdot (5.9)^{2}\times ({10}^{11})^{2} \\  & =320.252\times {10}^{22} \\  & =3.20252\times {10}^{24}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the equation, we get

$$
a=-\frac{3.20252\times {10}^{24}}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, since acceleration $a$ is the derivative of velocity $v,$ which is the derivative of distance $r,$ we can express acceleration as follows using the chain rule, treating $v$ as a function of $r$ along the trajectory:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{dv}{dt} \\  & =\frac{dr}{dt}\cdot \frac{dv}{dr} \\  & =v\frac{dv}{dr}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting this result into our equation, we obtain a separable differential equation for the velocity:

$$
v\frac{dv}{dr}=-\frac{3.20252\times {10}^{24}}{{r}^{2}}
$$
